**Observations:**
- Affected part: corn ear (two ears visible)
- Key visual features: dark brown/chocolate-colored masses of fungal material replacing or covering portions of the ear tissue, particularly at the base/tip of the ears
- The husk is pulled back revealing normal orange kernels on parts of the ear, but large dark dusty/powdery brown masses are present
- The brown masses look like fungal spore bodies — dark, dry, crumbly texture

**Reasoning:**
- The dark brown masses replacing ear tissue are characteristic of smut pathogens
- **Common Smut** (*Ustilago maydis*) produces galls that start white/gray and turn dark brown/black as they mature, releasing powdery spores — typically on ears, kernels, tassels
- **Head Smut** affects the tassel and ear, replacing them with smut masses
- The image shows what appears to be large smut galls on the ear, with dark brown powdery masses — this matches Common Smut very well, as it creates tumor-like galls on individual kernels/ear sections that rupture to expose dark spore masses
- The localized nature on the ear (not the entire plant/tassel replaced) points more to Common Smut than Head Smut
